title: FOMC Minutes — July 29–30, 2025
html:
Official minutes: HTML · PDF Local PDF: 2025-07-30 FOMC Minutes.pdf

Decision

The Committee held the federal funds target range at 4-1/4 to 4-1/2 percent, with interest on reserve balances at 4.4 percent. The vote was 9-2. Governors Michelle Bowman and Christopher Waller dissented in favor of a 25-basis-point cut; Adriana Kugler was absent. Bowman argued that, setting aside temporary tariff effects, inflation had moved "considerably closer" to target, the labor market showed "signs of less dynamism," and growth was slowing, so a gradual move toward neutral would hedge against weakness. Runoff continued with caps of $5 billion for Treasuries and $35 billion for agency debt and MBS.

Economic outlook

Staff said real GDP "expanded at a tepid pace in the first half of the year." GDP rose in Q2 after falling in Q1, with net exports swinging from a large drag to a large positive contribution, while private domestic final purchases slowed. Staff's outlook through 2027 was similar to June's. Participants said growth slowed in the first half, mainly from slower consumption and a decline in residential investment; several expected low growth in the second half.

Inflation

Total PCE inflation was about 2.5 percent and core about 2.7 percent in June, similar to a year earlier. Participants said inflation was "somewhat above" 2 percent, with tariff effects becoming visible in goods prices while services inflation kept slowing. A couple argued that, excluding tariffs, inflation was close to target. Longer-term expectations remained well anchored. Staff projected tariffs adding pressure in 2025 and somewhat in 2026, with inflation back at 2 percent by 2027.

Labor market

Unemployment fell to 4.1 percent in June. Total payroll gains were solid, but "private payroll gains stepped down noticeably." The vacancies-to-unemployed ratio was 1.1 and average hourly earnings rose 3.7 percent over the year. Participants saw employment at or near its maximum, though some noted slower, more concentrated job growth. Staff projected unemployment rising above its natural rate around year-end.

Financial markets & balance sheet

Equities rose, credit spreads narrowed and the dollar dipped slightly; S&P 500 valuations stayed above long-run averages. The debt-limit suspension ended with the One Big Beautiful Bill Act on July 4, and the Treasury General Account was expected to rise from $313 billion to about $500 billion by end-July. As a result, reserves were expected to fall in a sustained way for the first time since runoff began in 2022. Standing repo take-up hit $11.1 billion on June 30, the highest since inception. All participants agreed to keep shrinking holdings.

Risks participants flagged

  • A majority saw upside inflation risk, from tariffs and possible unanchoring of expectations, as the greater risk.
  • Downside employment risks: tighter financial conditions, a deeper housing downturn and AI possibly reducing employment.
  • Financial stability: elevated asset valuations, bank exposure to rising long-term yields, Treasury market dealer capacity, hedge funds, stablecoins and FX swaps.

What it signaled about next moves

The statement said the Committee would "carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks" and was "prepared to adjust the stance of monetary policy as appropriate." Several participants thought the current rate might not be far above neutral. Two governors already voting for a cut showed pressure building toward easing.

Read-through for SPY

  • Two governors dissenting in favor of a cut signaled easing was getting closer, a supportive sign for equities.
  • The majority still worried more about inflation, so the timing of cuts remained uncertain.
  • The minutes explicitly flagged above-average S&P 500 valuations as a financial-stability concern, a reminder that stocks were priced for good news.
